name: chem-g2-r2
context:
GAME TWO, ROUND TWO. Round one came back REVISE with one finding that mattered above all others: "If the beam search returns a margin of <5% over Greedy, you do not have a game; you have a simulation of decay." The beam search came back at 5.7%. So round one's design was dead on the auditor's own threshold, and this round is the record of finding out why and what the engine actually supports.

The suggested fix in round one was to run to equilibrium rather than a turn cap. I had already swept that — identical results at 20, 30, 45 and 60 turns — so it was rejected on evidence rather than adopted on authority.

─────────── FOUR MORE NEGATIVES BEFORE ANYTHING WORKED ───────────

NEGATIVE 6 — TIGHTENING THE BOARD DOES NOTHING. Hypothesis: the board is ergodic (299 legal moves at turn one), so any path lands in a similar soup; shrink the system and each move matters more. Swept live cells 36/20/12/8 crossed with common and rare target pools, 120 boards each. Common targets: 6.6% to 12.4% spread at EVERY board size, no trend. Board size is not the lever. (Rare targets did move — 28.9% to 37.5% — which is what sent the next measurement at the target pool rather than at the board.)

NEGATIVE 7 — AND IT WAS MY OWN INSTRUMENT, TWICE. Building the ladder properly surfaced two defects in my measurement rather than in the design:

  · the target objective scored WORSE at 60 turns than at 12. Players were making targets and then destroying them with later moves. A target sitting on the board is a hostage, not a score.
  · the beam search read its score as the HIGH-WATER MARK across the whole search while every other agent was scored on its FINAL board. That is not a ceiling, it is a different scoring rule wearing one, and it inflated the ceiling against every player it was compared to.

Both are the same fix and the fix is a design decision: AN ORDER, ONCE MET, IS DELIVERED — struck off, banked, and the molecule that met it leaves the board. That removes the hostage and makes high-water and final score the same number for everybody.

NEGATIVE 8 — DELIVERY THEN SATURATED THE OBJECTIVE. With three fixed orders and delivery, RANDOM play fills 2.48 of 3 and the entire ladder lands inside 1.2% of the ceiling. Too easy is as dead as too hard; the objective could not separate anyone. Replaced with a STANDING BOOK of three, refilled as they are filled, scored on THROUGHPUT.

─────────── WHAT THE ENGINE WAS THROWING AWAY ───────────

`bestRearrangement` enumerates every conservation-legal partition of a selected region and returns EXACTLY ONE: the most exothermic. Everything else is discarded before the player sees it. So a move is 'pick a region' and the products are decided for you — which is the structural reason greedy sits at 94–96% of ceiling on energy and why nothing above tried to fix it worked.

Census of what is discarded, 200 boards:

    reactants   alt partitions   distinct products   energy spread   runner-up within 10% of top
        2            1.4               1.4              120 kJ              11.2%
        3            2.5               2.5              268 kJ              47.5%
        4            4.8               4.8              470 kJ              69.5%

64.8% of regions have more than one alternative; the most on a single region was 27. At four reactants the RUNNER-UP IS INSIDE 10% OF THE TOP ENERGY 69.5% OF THE TIME — so spending a tenth of the energy to steer the products is a trade, not a blunder.

─────────── THE MEASUREMENT THAT DECIDES IT ───────────

Same board, same order stream, same seed. FLOOR = random legal move. ORDER-1 = one ply. ORDER-2 = two ply. CEILING = beam search. Orders filled in 12 turns, standing book of 3, rare pool, 220 boards.

    options per region   FLOOR   ORDER-1   ORDER-2   CEILING   headroom
         1 (the game today) 1.01    3.59      4.27      5.13      30.0%
         3                  1.50    5.08      6.33      7.64      33.5%

Giving the player three product options rather than one raises a naive player's throughput 41% and the ceiling 49%. Against the energy objective's 5.7%, headroom is 30–33%.

AND THE BREADTH SWEEP SET THE CAP RATHER THAN MY TASTE. Options per region 1/2/3/5/8/all: ORDER-2 reaches 5.37 at three options and is STILL 5.37 with all of them. Past three, only the beam search improves. That is a solver's mechanic and not a player's, so the menu is three and the reason is a measurement rather than a screen-size argument.

─────────── THE DESIGN THIS LEAVES ───────────

You are a SYNTHESIS LINE. Three orders stand open. The board is a closed system of molecules and conservation is a law: to make what is ordered you must find the atoms already on the board and route them there.

A move is a selection of 2–4 adjacent molecules AND A CHOICE OF WHAT TO MAKE FROM THEM, from the three best-paying conservation-legal rearrangements. Energy prices the choice — the top option always pays most, and taking a lower one to make what is ordered is the decision the whole game is built on. Fill an order and it ships, banks, and the next one arrives.

The board still winds down: greedy play manufactures thermodynamic sinks, doubles them from 6.7 to 15.0 of 36 cells, and dies at turn 9.5 with one legal move where random play has 37. That is now a cost you pay for throughput rather than the whole game.

CARRIES FROM ROUND ONE: conservation as a law; reactions scoring as a difference; the real bond-enthalpy and entropy tables; sinks as the decay clock; the ported deterministic PRNG and persona population; the dual-constraint gate.

DROPPED: temperature as a mechanic (round one, falsified — 0 of 400 boards changed their best move); scoring as a fraction of the board's energy ceiling (the objective is no longer energy); the no-turn-limit framing (throughput needs a horizon to be a rate).

questions.text: The core claim is that the game was never missing a mechanic — the engine already computed every legal partition and deleted all but the most exothermic, and exposing three of them is what opened 30-33% headroom where the energy objective had 5.7%. Is that a genuine mechanic or have I just widened the action space until a search had somewhere to go?

I capped the menu at three because ORDER-2 scores 5.37 at three options and 5.37 with all of them, so past three only the beam search improves. Is 'the naive player stops gaining' the right place to cut, or does that cap the skill ceiling exactly where the interesting play would start?

Two of this round's four negative results were defects in MY instrument, not in the design — a hostage-target scoring rule and a beam search scored on high-water while players were scored on their final board. Both were found by building the ladder rather than by review. What else in this measurement set should I distrust?

Delivering an order removes the molecule and refills the cell. That is the rule that rescued the objective from saturation in one direction and from decay in the other. What does it cost me — what does a player learn from it that is not true of chemistry?
Farkle's question is 'again?'. This game's is 'what do I make from these four?'. Name the strongest reason a player would find that a worse question rather than a different one.
